974.title: Napoleon's Sanhedrin (1807)
974.hook: Napoleon questions Jewish leaders about loyalty and law
974.howItsDone: The Talmudic principle dina de-malkhuta dina is still taught in Jewish law today, as the basis for keeping a country's civil laws, such as paying taxes, alongside the commandments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a vote in Paris made Jews citizens, as individuals. Your line was a door opened, with a price. Today, an emperor wants to know what those citizens really think.

A list of questions lands on the table of Jewish leaders gathered in Paris. It comes from the emperor, Napoleon, and it isn't about theology. Does your law allow a man more than one wife? Is a Jewish divorce valid without the state's courts? May a Jew marry a Christian? Do you consider the French your brothers? Is France your country, and will you defend it? Underneath them all lies one question: can you be fully Jewish and fully French at the same time? Today, Napoleon's Sanhedrin.
screen: `A LIST FROM THE EMPEROR.` → `WIVES, DIVORCE, MARRIAGE, BROTHERS.` → `CAN YOU BE BOTH?`

segments.voice: Napoleon first called an assembly of Jewish notables, rabbis and lay leaders, to answer his questions. Then, to give their answers religious weight, he did something theatrical. He summoned a Grand Sanhedrin, borrowing the name of the ancient high court of Jewish law in Jerusalem, a court of the distant past. How did they answer? Carefully, and within Jewish law. A man may have only one wife; they pointed to the old ban on taking more. A religious divorce should follow a civil one. France is our country and we will defend it; the French are our brothers. On marrying Christians they walked a narrow line: such marriages were valid in civil law, while rabbis would not perform them. Under many answers lay one principle from the Talmud, a saying of the sage Shmuel in Aramaic: dina de-malkhuta dina, the law of the kingdom is the law. In matters like taxes, property and civil order, Jewish law itself tells Jews to keep the law of the land. That principle was not invented for Napoleon; it was already in the Talmud. What the Sanhedrin did was draw a line with it. Here, in civil life, the state's law binds us. There, in the commandments between a person and God, our Torah does. The emperor wanted loyalty. The assembly gave it, and kept back something that was not theirs to give. A loyal question can make you say clearly where your loyalties lie, and where they stop.
screen: `AN ASSEMBLY, THEN A GRAND SANHEDRIN.` · `CAREFUL ANSWERS WITHIN JEWISH LAW.` · `DINA DE-MALKHUTA DINA.` · then, large: `WHERE LOYALTY LIES, AND WHERE IT STOPS.`

segments.voice: Think of a question about where your loyalties lie, one someone asked you or one you've been avoiding: to a job, a family, a friend, a community, a belief. Let it sit, then answer the way the Sanhedrin did: carefully, without flattering anyone, saying clearly what you will give and what you will keep; you don't have to say it out loud.
Napoleon's Sanhedrin. The Jewish assembly the emperor summoned to answer his questions about loyalty and law, and the Grand Sanhedrin that confirmed its answers. Today's word.
Your line: loyal questions. The Talmud already had an answer ready. Day nine hundred seventy-four, done.

975.title: Reform begins
975.hook: German Jews change services: sermons, organs, the vernacular
975.howItsDone: Reform synagogues today commonly hold services that mix Hebrew with the local language and include instrumental music, while Orthodox synagogues keep a traditional Hebrew service without instruments on Shabbat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Napoleon's Sanhedrin: the law of the kingdom is the law, and a careful line drawn with it. Your line was loyal questions. Today, German Jews ask about their own synagogues.

A Sabbath morning in a German town. Jewish families walk in to pray, and the room sounds different. There is an organ. A choir sings. Some prayers are in German, the language these families now speak at home and at work. Then a man stands and gives a sermon, in German, polished and earnest. Some are moved to tears; for once they understand every word. Others walk out shaken; to them this is no longer the synagogue of their parents. Today, Reform begins.
screen: `AN ORGAN, A CHOIR.` → `PRAYERS IN GERMAN.` → `TEARS, AND PEOPLE WALKING OUT.`

segments.voice: The new citizens of yesterday's story faced a real worry. Their children were learning German, going to German schools, entering German professions, and some were drifting away from Judaism altogether, finding the synagogue long, hard to follow, and out of step with the rest of their week. A group of German Jews decided the answer was to change the service itself. A layman named Israel Jacobson built a house of prayer with an organ and held services with German hymns and German sermons. In Hamburg, a congregation opened a temple with its own new prayer book: shorter, partly in German, and with changes to some prayers about the return to Zion. They wanted worship that was dignified, understandable and modern. The organ became a symbol of the whole fight. Supporters could point to Psalm one hundred fifty, as the King James Bible renders it: "Praise him with stringed instruments and organs." Opponents answered that playing an instrument on the Sabbath breaks the Sabbath, that the organ imitated the church, and that the prayers were not anyone's to rewrite. Traditional rabbis published rulings against the Hamburg prayer book. The reformers feared losing the young to the world. The traditionalists feared losing the prayers their parents had said, word for word. The Reform movement grew out of these first changes, and so did new ways of defending tradition, which we'll meet tomorrow. And the question the organ raised, what may change in a service and who decides, would be argued in synagogue after synagogue.
screen: `CHILDREN DRIFTING AWAY.` · `ORGAN, CHOIR, GERMAN SERMONS.` · `PRAISE HIM WITH ORGANS?` · then, large: `TWO FEARS, ONE SYNAGOGUE.`

segments.voice: Think of something that changed around you, a family tradition done a new way, a community that modernized, and let yourself feel both sides: what was gained, what was lost, who welcomed it and who walked out quietly. You don't have to decide who was right; just hold the tears of the one who finally understood and the shock of the one who no longer recognized the room.
Jacobson. The layman who built the first Reform-style house of prayer, with an organ, German hymns, and sermons the young could understand. Today's word.
Your line: tears, and people walking out. Under each side's argument was a fear of losing something. See you tomorrow.

976.title: Samson Raphael Hirsch
976.hook: Torah joined with worldly life, a founder of modern Orthodoxy
976.howItsDone: Modern Orthodox Jewish schools today commonly teach a dual curriculum of Torah and general studies, and some trace that model to Hirsch's motto, Torah im derekh eretz.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Reform began with Jacobson's organ in the synagogue. Your line was tears, and people walking out. Today, a rabbi who answered the same worry another way.

A schoolboy's bag in Frankfurt. Inside it, a book of the Torah in Hebrew. Next to it, a German grammar, a geometry book, a history of the ancient world. He'll study all of them today, in one building, from teachers who keep the Sabbath and the dietary laws without bending them. Nobody there thinks the geometry is a threat to the Torah, or the Torah an excuse to skip the geometry. The rabbi who built this school believed both belonged in one bag. His name was Samson Raphael Hirsch.
screen: `ONE SCHOOLBAG.` → `THE TORAH AND A GEOMETRY BOOK.` → `BOTH BELONG IN ONE BAG.`

segments.voice: Hirsch faced the same crisis as yesterday's reformers: young German Jews drifting from Judaism as they entered German life. But he drew the opposite conclusion about the law. The Torah, he said, was not something to adjust to the times; it was the measure by which the times are judged. So he would not change the service or loosen the commandments. Yet he was no stranger to the modern world. He wrote fine German prose, admired German poets, and wanted Jewish children to learn science, languages and history alongside Torah. His motto came from the Mishnah. In Pirkei Avot, Rabban Gamliel, the son of Rabbi Judah the Prince, says Torah study is beautiful together with derekh eretz, the way of the land, meaning a worldly occupation, because the effort of both keeps a person from sin. Hirsch took those words, Torah im derekh eretz, and made them a whole program. For him, derekh eretz meant more than a job: the whole of a cultured, working, civic life, lived inside the commandments rather than beside them. A Jew could be a doctor, a merchant, a reader of poetry and a citizen, and keep every law of the Sabbath while doing it. He built schools in Frankfurt to teach exactly that, and wrote a long commentary on the Torah that is still read. People often name him as a founder of what came to be called modern Orthodoxy. Not every traditional rabbi shared his openness to secular learning, and Orthodox Jews still discuss how far his program reaches. But his answer was clear: keep the Torah whole, and bring the world inside it.
screen: `THE TORAH IS THE MEASURE OF THE TIMES.` · `NO CHANGE TO THE LAW.` · `TORAH WITH THE WAY OF THE LAND.` · then, large: `BRING THE WORLD INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: Think of the ordinary work in front of you today and one teaching you hold dear, from the Torah or wherever you draw wisdom: honesty, rest, kindness to the stranger. Ask where in that work the teaching could live, not beside it but inside it.
Hirsch. A Frankfurt rabbi who taught Torah im derekh eretz, Torah joined with worldly life, and is often named a founder of modern Orthodoxy. Today's word.
Your line: torah with the world. The geometry and the Torah fit in one bag. Day nine hundred seventy-six.

977.title: Zacharias Frankel
977.hook: a rabbi walks out of a meeting and starts looking for a middle path between tradition and history
977.howItsDone: Conservative Jewish communities study Jewish law alongside its history, and their rabbis make rulings on change through committees that weigh both the tradition and the practice of the community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samson Raphael Hirsch, and your line: torah with the world. The law given whole, lived fully in modern life. Today, another German rabbi of the same time, who drew the line in a different place.

A room full of rabbis in Frankfurt, deep in a long argument. The question sounds small: does Jewish prayer have to be in Hebrew? The meeting leans toward an answer: Hebrew is welcome, but not required. One rabbi, Zacharias Frankel, listens, gathers his papers and leaves. He doesn't cross over to the other camp either. He spends the rest of his life looking for a road between the two camps in that room.
screen: `A ROOM OF RABBIS IN FRANKFURT.` → `MUST PRAYER BE IN HEBREW?` → `ONE RABBI WALKS OUT.`

segments.voice: By Frankel's day, German Jews were splitting into camps. The reformers, two days ago, wanted to change prayer and practice to fit modern life. Hirsch, yesterday, held that the law was given whole, to be lived fully inside the modern world. Frankel agreed fully with neither. He was a scholar of history. He read the Mishnah and the Talmud the way a historian reads, asking when a law took shape, and how, and why. He was ready to say that Jewish law had grown and changed over time. That sounded like the reformers. But he drew a different conclusion. If the law grew inside the life of the people, then the people's long practice carries real weight. Hebrew in prayer was not a habit to drop. It was part of the living body of Judaism. So change could come, but slowly, from inside, with respect for what the people had actually kept. His name for this was positive-historical Judaism. Positive, because the tradition is given and real. Historical, because it has a history and is still moving. He went on to lead a new rabbinical seminary in Breslau, where students learned both the texts and the methods of history. Conservative Judaism, which grew later, looks back on him as a forerunner. Jeremiah has a line that fits his instinct. The prophet tells the people to stand in the ways and look, and to "ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein." Not frozen where the roads meet, and not running off in a new direction. Ask the old paths, then walk.
screen: `TWO CAMPS IN GERMANY.` · `LAW WITH A HISTORY.` · `POSITIVE-HISTORICAL JUDAISM.` · then, large: `ASK FOR THE OLD PATHS.`

978.title: The Mortara affair (1858)
978.hook: a Jewish boy is taken from his parents in Bologna
978.howItsDone: Jewish historians and teachers retell the Mortara case as part of the story of emancipation, and it is often studied alongside the fight for religious freedom and the rights of parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zacharias Frankel, and your line: the middle path. Change slowly, from inside. Today there is no middle path to find, only a family and a door.

Evening, in a house in Bologna. Momolo and Marianna Mortara have put their children to bed. There is a knock. Police of the Papal States are at the door, with an order to take one of the boys, Edgardo. The parents beg. They are given a little time, and then the boy is carried out of the house. His family will spend years trying to bring him back. Today's story is hard, and it is told here plainly.
screen: `A HOUSE IN BOLOGNA.` → `A KNOCK AT NIGHT.` → `EDGARDO IS CARRIED OUT.`

segments.voice: Bologna was then ruled by the pope as a worldly king, and church law was the law of the land. Under that law, a child who had been baptized a Catholic could not be raised by Jewish parents. The family had a Christian servant girl. She said that years before, when Edgardo was a baby and very sick, she had secretly sprinkled water on him and said the words of baptism, afraid he would die. She told no one at the time. When the story reached church officials, they ruled the boy was now a Catholic, and sent the police. Edgardo was taken to Rome and raised in a house for converts, under the protection of Pope Pius the Ninth himself. His father traveled, wrote, pleaded. Jewish communities in other countries took up the case. Newspapers across Europe and in America printed it, and readers who were not Jewish were troubled too. Governments sent protests. The pope refused to send him home. The ending is harder still. Edgardo grew up inside the Church and became a Catholic priest. When the Papal States later fell, he was old enough to choose, and he chose to stay. He never returned to his parents' faith. Jews remember the case as a wound, and Catholic writers have argued about it in their own way. The Torah knows a father's grief like this. When Jacob is told his son Joseph is gone, he tears his clothes and mourns, while the boy is alive and far away in a foreign land. Genesis gives that grief one short line: "And his father wept for him."
screen: `THE POPE AS A WORLDLY KING.` · `A SECRET BAPTISM.` · `A CASE THE WORLD READ.` · then, large: `AND HIS FATHER WEPT FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: Bring Edgardo's family to mind: his father traveling and writing, his mother at home, the other children in the next room. Think of anyone you know who is waiting for someone who hasn't come home, and hold the waiting for a moment without trying to end it. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words.
Mortara. The family name of Edgardo, a Jewish boy in Bologna taken from his parents by the Papal States after a secret baptism was claimed. Today's word.
Your line: the taken child. Thank you for staying with a hard story today. See you tomorrow.

979.title: Yemen
979.hook: an ancient community with its own prayers, melodies and Torah readings
979.howItsDone: In Yemenite synagogues the Torah is read verse by verse with the Aramaic Targum, often chanted by a child, and prayers follow the Tiklal prayer book with melodies handed down in families.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mortara affair, and your line: the taken child. A family's long grief. Today the story turns south and east, away from Europe, to the wider Jewish world.

A Shabbat morning in a Yemenite synagogue. The Torah scroll is open. A reader chants a verse in Hebrew, in a melody of its own, rising and falling. Then he stops, and a young boy beside him chants the same verse again, this time in Aramaic. Verse by verse, Hebrew, then Aramaic, all the way through the reading. Nobody is rushing, not the reader and not the boy. Today, the Jews of Yemen.
screen: `A SHABBAT MORNING.` → `A VERSE IN HEBREW.` → `THE SAME VERSE IN ARAMAIC.`

segments.voice: Yemen sits at the bottom corner of the Arabian peninsula. Jews lived there for a very long time, and tradition tells of their arrival in the days of the Bible. Far from the big centers of Jewish learning, they kept their own ways. First, the reading. That Aramaic voice is the Targum, an ancient translation of the Torah. In many places it stopped being read aloud in the synagogue. Yemenite Jews kept the custom, and a child often reads the Targum, so the young learn by doing. Second, the prayers. Yemenite Jews have their own prayer book, the Tiklal, with its own order and melodies, passed down mostly by ear, in families, in the same small synagogues. Third, the poetry. A beloved Yemenite poet, Shalom Shabazi, wrote songs still sung at weddings and Shabbat tables, mixing Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic. When the State of Israel was new, Jews from Yemen were flown there in an airlift people named after a verse from Exodus, where God tells Israel: "I bore you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto Myself." People who had never seen an airplane, tradition says, recognized it from that verse. The melodies came along, and singers from Yemenite families carried them into new music. And in Yemenite synagogues in Israel, a child may still stand beside the reader, ready with the Aramaic.
screen: `A CORNER OF ARABIA.` · `THE TARGUM READ ALOUD.` · `THE TIKLAL AND SHABAZI'S SONGS.` · then, large: `ON EAGLES' WINGS.`

segments.voice: Bring back the synagogue: the Hebrew verse, then the boy's voice with the same verse in Aramaic. Let your breath follow that pattern, one breath to hear, one to repeat. Then think of one thing you learned by repeating after someone older, and hold them in mind.
Yemen. Home to a Jewish community that kept the Targum read aloud, its own prayer book, the Tiklal, and the songs of Shalom Shabazi. Today's word.
Your line: a child reads the Targum. Old ways, kept by ear and by doing. Until tomorrow.

980.title: Morocco
980.hook: the night Passover ends, Moroccan Jewish homes open their doors to neighbors for Mimouna
980.howItsDone: On the night Passover ends, Moroccan Jewish families set a table with mufleta pancakes, honey, milk and greenery, visit from house to house with blessings, and in Israel the next day often brings large outdoor picnics.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yemen, and your line: a child reads the Targum. Old customs, kept by ear. Today, across North Africa to Morocco, and the last day of this week.

Passover ends at nightfall. For a week, no bread in the house. And in Moroccan Jewish homes, almost as the last blessing is said, the kitchen comes alive. Flour comes out. Thin pancakes go into the pan, eaten warm with butter and honey. The table fills with sweets, fresh milk, green stalks of wheat. The front door stays open, and the neighbors come in, Jewish and not. Today's word is the name of that night.
screen: `PASSOVER ENDS AT NIGHTFALL.` → `PANCAKES WITH BUTTER AND HONEY.` → `THE DOOR STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Mimouna. Nobody is quite sure where the name comes from. Some connect it to Maimon, the father of Maimonides, said to have died around this time of year. Others hear in it the Hebrew emunah, faith, or an Arabic word for good fortune. The custom is clearer than the name. On Mimouna night, families set a table like a wish for the year ahead: honey for sweetness, milk for plenty, wheat for a good harvest, sometimes a fish for blessing. Guests walk from house to house, greeting each other with a Judeo-Arabic blessing for success and good luck. Then there are the neighbors. In Morocco, tradition says, Muslim neighbors would bring flour, butter and milk to Jewish homes as Passover ended, since their own kitchens had none, and stay to eat. The party became a meeting place. When Moroccan Jews moved to Israel, they brought Mimouna with them, and the open door became an open park, with picnics that welcome whoever comes. The Torah gives a simple rule that this night acts out: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Mimouna turns it into flour, pancakes and an unlocked door. Look back at this week, too. A Sanhedrin called by Napoleon. Reform beginning. Hirsch joining Torah with the world. Frankel's middle path. The Mortaras' terrible night. The Targum in Yemen. And now a door in Morocco, wide open after Passover.
screen: `A NAME NOBODY IS SURE OF.` · `A TABLE LIKE A WISH.` · `NEIGHBORS AT THE DOOR.` · then, large: `AS THYSELF.`
